title: Static Site Generation (SSG)
summary: **Static Site Generation (SSG)** pre-renders a route to HTML once **at build time** and serves it from a CDN, giving the fastest possible first paint, the cheapest hosting, and excellent SEO — perfect for content that rarely changes.

subtopics.title: What SSG actually does
subtopics.explanation: At build time, Next.js runs your Server Component, fetches its (cacheable) data, renders React to HTML, and writes static files. Those files are pushed to a CDN and served instantly to every visitor without any server work per request. In the App Router this is the default for routes whose data is cacheable.

subtopics.title: The cacheable-fetch default
subtopics.explanation: In the App Router a plain fetch is cached by default, so a route that only uses such fetches is statically generated automatically — you don't opt in. The page is built once and the result is reused for every request, which is why SSG is the framework's default for stable, shareable content.
subtopics.example: const data = await fetch('https://api/posts'); // cached -> SSG

subtopics.title: generateStaticParams for dynamic routes
subtopics.explanation: For a dynamic segment like blog/[slug], you tell Next.js which paths to pre-build by exporting generateStaticParams, which returns the list of param values. Next then statically generates one HTML file per slug at build time, so every known page is CDN-fast.

subtopics.title: force-static route config
subtopics.explanation: You can explicitly opt a route segment into static rendering with a route segment config export. This guarantees the route is built statically (and uncached data is treated as empty/cached), which is handy to document intent or to prevent accidental dynamic rendering.
subtopics.example:
// top of the route file
export const dynamic = 'force-static';

subtopics.title: Pros: CDN speed, cost, SEO
subtopics.explanation: Because pages are pre-built files served from a CDN, TTFB is minimal, hosting is nearly free, and the system scales effortlessly to huge traffic. Crawlers receive complete HTML, so SEO is excellent. There is no per-request server compute at all for static routes.
subtopics.example: // Pre-built HTML from CDN = fastest TTFB, cheapest, infinitely scalable

subtopics.title: Cons: stale until rebuild
subtopics.explanation: The fundamental trade-off is freshness: the HTML reflects the data as of the last build and stays frozen until you redeploy. If content changes between builds, visitors see stale data. For occasionally-changing content, ISR (SSG + revalidation) solves this without giving up static delivery.
subtopics.example: // Content frozen at build time -> redeploy (or use ISR) to update

subtopics.title: When to use SSG
subtopics.explanation: Reach for SSG when content is public, shareable across all users, and changes rarely or only at deploy time: marketing pages, documentation, landing pages, changelogs, and blog posts. If it changes often, prefer ISR; if it's per-user or always-fresh, use SSR.
subtopics.example: Marketing, docs, landing pages, blogs -> SSG

foundations.overview: Static Site Generation pre-renders a route to HTML at build time and serves the resulting files from a CDN, so every visitor gets identical, instantly-delivered, fully-formed markup with zero per-request server work. In the Next.js App Router it is the default strategy for routes whose data is cacheable, making it the cheapest and fastest way to serve stable, public content.
foundations.formalDefinition: SSG (static rendering) is the strategy where a route's HTML is generated once at build time using cacheable data and served as static files, rather than rendered per request. In Next.js it is the default for cacheable fetches, configured for dynamic routes via generateStaticParams, and can be forced via export const dynamic = 'force-static'.
foundations.whyItMatters: SSG delivers the best possible performance and cost profile for content that doesn't need per-request freshness. Knowing that it's the App Router default — and how to pre-build dynamic routes — is fundamental to building fast, cheap, SEO-friendly Next.js apps.
foundations.mentalModel: Picture printing a magazine: you typeset and print every page once (build), then hand identical copies to all readers (CDN). It's incredibly fast and cheap to distribute, but the content is fixed until you print the next edition (redeploy).
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser receives a complete, pre-built HTML file straight from the nearest CDN edge, painting content almost instantly, then downloads JavaScript to hydrate it into an interactive React tree. There is no waiting on a server to render.
foundations.realWorldUsage: A company marketing homepage, a documentation site, a product landing page, a changelog, or a blog whose posts only change when redeployed — all served as pre-built static HTML.
foundations.businessImpact: SSG maximizes Core Web Vitals and SEO, which drive organic traffic and conversion, while slashing hosting cost to near-zero and removing scaling concerns — the best ROI for stable public content.
foundations.engineeringImpact: SSG removes per-request server logic for those routes, simplifying operations and eliminating a class of latency/scaling problems; the main engineering work shifts to the build (and to deciding which routes are safely static).
foundations.performanceImpact: Static files served from a CDN have the lowest achievable TTFB and FCP and scale to unlimited traffic without added latency. The only cost is build time, which grows with the number of pre-rendered pages.
commonUseCases: Blog posts and articles that change at deploy time
Changelogs, about pages, and other stable public content

commonMisconceptions.myth: SSG can only be used for a few hard-coded pages, not dynamic routes.
commonMisconceptions.reality: generateStaticParams pre-builds one static page per param value, so thousands of blog posts or products can be statically generated at build time.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Static pages can never update without a full redeploy.
commonMisconceptions.reality: ISR adds a revalidate window so static pages refresh in the background; SSG is just the default, and you can layer revalidation on top without giving up CDN delivery.

steps.name: Build starts
steps.detail: During next build, Next.js renders each static route once, running its Server Components and cacheable fetches to produce finished HTML.

steps.name: Enumerate dynamic paths
steps.detail: For dynamic routes like blog/[slug], generateStaticParams returns the list of params, so Next pre-builds one HTML file per known path.

steps.name: Write static files
steps.detail: The rendered HTML (plus JSON for hydration) is written out as static assets — no server code runs per request.

steps.name: Deploy to CDN
steps.detail: Those files are pushed to a CDN, replicated to edge locations close to users worldwide.

steps.name: Serve + hydrate
steps.detail: A request hits the nearest edge, which returns the pre-built HTML instantly; the browser then downloads JS and hydrates it.

codeLab.title: Will this route be statically generated?
codeLab.instructions: For each route description, decide whether Next.js statically generates it (SSG) and why. Edit the component to fill in your answers, then Run. (Plain cached fetch; dynamic route with generateStaticParams; no-store fetch; force-static export.)
codeLab.expectedOutput: Your static-vs-dynamic call for each route with a reason.
hints: A route is static if all its data is cacheable and it reads no request-only data.
Default fetch / generateStaticParams / force-static -> SSG; no-store / cookies / headers -> SSR.

debuggingLab.title: My blog post pages aren't being pre-built
debuggingLab.symptom: A blog/[slug] route renders dynamically (slow TTFB, server work per request) even though the posts are public and stable, because no static params were provided.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Without generateStaticParams, Next.js doesn't know which slugs exist at build time, so it can't pre-render the dynamic pages and falls back to rendering them on demand. The fetch is cacheable, but for a dynamic segment you must enumerate the params to statically generate each page.
commonMistakes: Forgetting generateStaticParams on a dynamic route you want pre-built.
Assuming a cacheable fetch alone is enough to pre-build a dynamic [slug] route.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Export generateStaticParams returning every slug so Next.js pre-builds one static page per post.

theory.question: What is Static Site Generation in Next.js and why is it the App Router default?
theory.directAnswer: SSG pre-renders a route to HTML once at build time and serves the resulting files from a CDN, with no per-request server work. It's the App Router default because a plain fetch is cached by default, so any route using only cacheable data is statically generated automatically. You pre-build dynamic routes with generateStaticParams and can force static rendering with export const dynamic = 'force-static'.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A build-time rendering strategy producing static HTML served from a CDN.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Stable public content doesn't need per-request rendering, so building once gives the best speed and cost.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: At build, Next renders cacheable Server Components to HTML files; generateStaticParams enumerates dynamic paths; the CDN serves the files.

theory.whyImportant: SSG is the cheapest, fastest way to serve public content and is the framework's default; understanding it is foundational to right-sizing rendering.
theory.realWorldExample: A documentation site builds every page to static HTML at deploy time and serves them from a CDN, achieving near-instant loads and minimal cost.

nestedTopics.title: Default caching
nestedTopics.explanation: A plain fetch is cached, so the route is static unless something opts it out.

nestedTopics.title: generateStaticParams
nestedTopics.explanation: Returns the param values to pre-build one static page per dynamic path.

nestedTopics.title: force-static
nestedTopics.explanation: Route segment config that explicitly forces static rendering.

followUps.question: How do you statically generate a dynamic route like blog/[slug]?
followUps.answer: Export generateStaticParams returning the list of slugs; Next pre-builds one static HTML file per slug at build time.

followUps.question: What opts a route out of SSG?
followUps.answer: An uncached (no-store) fetch, a dynamic function like cookies()/headers(), or export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic' makes it SSR instead.

theory.question: What are the trade-offs of SSG, and how do you handle content that changes after build?
theory.directAnswer: SSG's strengths are CDN-fast TTFB, near-zero hosting cost, effortless scaling, and great SEO; its one weakness is freshness — the HTML is frozen at the last build and stale until you redeploy. For content that changes after build, you add a revalidate window (ISR) so static pages refresh in the background, or use on-demand revalidation; for per-user/always-fresh content you use SSR instead.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A look at SSG's cost/freshness trade-off and the upgrade path to ISR.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Building once trades freshness for speed and cost; many sites need a middle ground.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: ISR keeps static delivery but regenerates pages after a revalidate interval or on demand.

theory.whyImportant: It tests whether you understand SSG's only real limitation and the standard remedy (ISR), a common interview discriminator.
theory.realWorldExample: A blog uses SSG for instant loads but adds revalidate: 3600 so edits appear within an hour without a full redeploy.

nestedTopics.title: Build time
nestedTopics.explanation: SSG cost shifts to build duration, which grows with the number of pre-rendered pages.

nestedTopics.title: ISR upgrade
nestedTopics.explanation: Adding revalidate keeps CDN delivery while allowing periodic background refresh.

followUps.question: When is SSG the wrong choice?
followUps.answer: When content is per-user or must always be current (use SSR), or when it changes frequently enough that staleness matters and rebuilding everything is impractical (use ISR).

scenario.question: A docs site has thousands of pages and builds are getting slow; some pages are rarely visited. How do you keep SSG benefits without a painful build?
scenario.directAnswer: Keep the popular, stable pages statically generated, but avoid pre-building every rarely-visited page up front. Use generateStaticParams to pre-build the high-traffic subset and let the rest be generated on first request and then cached (ISR-style on-demand generation), or add a revalidate window so pages refresh without rebuilding everything. This preserves CDN-fast delivery while bounding build time.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A build-scalability problem for a large static site.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Pre-rendering every page at build doesn't scale as page counts grow.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Pre-build a subset and defer the long tail to on-demand static generation with caching/revalidation.

scenario.whyImportant: It shows you can balance build cost against delivery performance for large content sites — a real production concern.

nestedTopics.title: Partial pre-building
nestedTopics.explanation: Return only high-value params from generateStaticParams; generate the rest on demand.

nestedTopics.title: On-demand generation
nestedTopics.explanation: Pages built on first request are then cached and served statically thereafter.

followUps.question: How do you confirm which pages were pre-built?
followUps.answer: The next build output lists generated static routes (○) and shows counts; inspect it and cache HIT/MISS in production.

coding.question: Write an App Router dynamic blog route that is statically generated for every post at build time.
coding.thoughtProcess: To statically generate a [slug] route I must tell Next which slugs exist, via generateStaticParams. The page itself uses a default (cached) fetch so it stays static. I'll enumerate slugs from the API and render each post. I can also force static explicitly for clarity.
coding.lineByLine: generateStaticParams returns one object per slug, so Next pre-builds one static HTML file per post at build time. The page's fetch uses the default cache, so each generated page stays static (no per-request rendering). The optional force-static export documents and guarantees static rendering. The component renders the post's title and HTML.
coding.timeComplexity: Build-time work is O(number of posts); per-request serving is O(1) from the CDN.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(number of pre-built pages) of static output.

alternativeApproaches.title: Add revalidation (ISR)
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Keep static delivery but refresh periodically.
alternativeApproaches.code: export const revalidate = 3600; // regenerate at most hourly

followUps.question: What happens if a request comes in for a slug not returned by generateStaticParams?
followUps.answer: By default Next will generate it on demand (then cache it); you can opt out with export const dynamicParams = false to return a 404 for unknown slugs.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Make static the default: any public, shareable, stable route should be SSG, served from the CDN with no per-request compute. Pre-build dynamic routes with generateStaticParams, and reserve SSR/ISR for content that's per-user or changes after build. Keep Client Components small so static pages ship minimal hydration JS.
productionDeepDive.performance: Static files from a CDN give the lowest TTFB/FCP and scale to unlimited traffic. The cost moves to build time, which grows with page count — bound it by pre-building only high-value pages and deferring the long tail to on-demand generation. Cache build data and parallelize fetches to speed builds.
productionDeepDive.security: Static pages contain only what you render at build, so be careful not to bake secrets or per-user data into them; anything sensitive or request-specific must be SSR/CSR. There's no per-request server code on static routes, which reduces attack surface.
productionDeepDive.scaling: SSG scales almost for free because the CDN absorbs traffic; there's no origin server load per request. The scaling concern is build time and the number of generated pages, not runtime capacity.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Keep generateStaticParams as the single source of truth for which pages exist, and make force-static/revalidate explicit so reviewers can see a route's strategy. Document why any route is dynamic instead of static.
productionDeepDive.observability: The next build output lists static routes (○) and page counts; track build duration and CDN cache HIT rates. Watch for routes that unexpectedly became dynamic, which inflate cost and latency.

caseStudies.problem: Large volumes of public, stable pages must load instantly and rank well, at minimal cost.
caseStudies.solution: Statically generate every page at build (generateStaticParams for dynamic routes) and serve from a CDN.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Content is frozen until rebuild and large sites have long builds, mitigated by ISR and partial pre-building.
caseStudies.lessons: Default to SSG for stable public content; layer ISR only where freshness or build time demands it.

keyTakeaways: SSG pre-renders a route to HTML once at build time and serves it from a CDN — the fastest TTFB, cheapest hosting, and effortless scaling for stable public content.
It's the App Router default: a plain (cached) fetch makes a route statically generated automatically.
Pre-build dynamic routes with generateStaticParams (one static page per param) and force it explicitly with export const dynamic = 'force-static'.
SSG's one weakness is staleness — content is frozen until rebuild; add ISR (revalidate) for periodic freshness without losing CDN delivery.
Use SSG for marketing, docs, and blogs; use ISR for occasionally-changing content and SSR for per-user or always-fresh pages.
